law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: The supreme law of Pakistan. It sets up the State, protects fundamental rights (Part II, Chapter 1), and lets people go to the High Courts and the Supreme Court when those rights are violated.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: No person shall be deprived of life or liberty save in accordance with law.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: Nobody can be deprived of life or liberty except through a process allowed by law. The State cannot simply take away your freedom or your life on its own say-so.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
section: Article 10 Safeguards as to arrest and detention
text:
(1) No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest, nor shall he be denied the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice.
(2) Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before a magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the nearest magistrate, and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
section: Article 10 Safeguards as to arrest and detention
text: If you are arrested, you must be told the reasons as soon as possible, and you have the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer you choose. You must be brought before a magistrate within 24 hours (not counting the travel time to court) and cannot be kept longer without the magistrate's permission. Only sub-articles (1) and (2) are bundled here; the later sub-articles deal with preventive detention and have special rules.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: For the determination of his civil rights and obligations or in any criminal charge against him a person shall be entitled to a fair trial and due process.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: In deciding your civil rights and obligations, or any criminal charge against you, you are entitled to a fair trial and due process — for example, to be heard before a decision is made against you.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
section: Article 14 Inviolability of dignity of man, etc.
text:
(1) The dignity of man and, subject to law, the privacy of home, shall be inviolable.
(2) No person shall be subjected to torture for the purpose of extracting evidence.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
section: Article 14 Inviolability of dignity of man, etc.
text: A person's dignity is protected, and so, subject to law, is the privacy of the home. Nobody may be tortured to extract evidence.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: Every citizen shall have the right to have access to information in all matters of public importance subject to regulation and reasonable restrictions imposed by law.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: Every citizen has a right of access to information in all matters of public importance, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law. Laws such as the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017 explain how to ask.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text:
(1) All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law.
(2) There shall be no discrimination on the basis of sex alone.
(3) Nothing in this Article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the protection of women and children.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: Every citizen is equal before the law and has the right to equal protection of the law. The law cannot discriminate on the basis of sex alone, but the State may make special provisions to protect women and children.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of five to sixteen years in such manner as may be determined by law.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: The State must provide free and compulsory education to children aged five to sixteen, in the way the law decides.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
section: Article 184(3) Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (fundamental rights)
text: The Supreme Court can directly hear a matter of public importance that involves enforcing fundamental rights. This is the source of what is often called suo motu or public-interest jurisdiction. Read the exact wording and conditions on the official source.

law: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973
text: A High Court can issue orders called writs (for example habeas corpus to release a person held unlawfully, or mandamus to direct an official to do a legal duty) when there is no other adequate remedy and a government authority has acted without lawful authority. This is the usual route for “constitutional petitions”. Read the full Article for its conditions.

The main criminal code. It defines offences such as theft, cheating, criminal intimidation and offences against the body, and sets out punishments. Procedure (how cases are registered and tried) is in the Code of Criminal Procedure.

section: Section 34 Acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention
text: When a criminal act is done by several people sharing a common intention, each of them can be held responsible as if he had done it alone.

Deals with the punishment for intentional murder (qatl-i-amd). The consequences depend on the type of case (for example qisas or tazir) and on later amendments, so read the current text with a lawyer's help.

Theft means dishonestly taking movable property out of someone's possession without consent. This section sets the punishment (imprisonment, fine, or both). Check the current text for the exact limits.

section: Section 420 Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property
text: Applies when a person cheats someone and thereby dishonestly makes them hand over property or sign a valuable document. It is commonly invoked in fraud and false-promise cases.

Threatening someone with injury to their person, reputation or property (or that of someone they care about) to alarm them or make them do or not do something is criminal intimidation. More serious threats carry higher punishment.

section: Section 509 Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman
text: Addresses words, sounds, gestures or objects intended to insult the modesty of a woman or invade her privacy. Harassment in digital spaces may also fall under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016.

The procedural law for criminal cases: how a crime is reported (FIR), investigated, how arrests, remand and bail work, and how trials and appeals proceed. Several amendments and related laws apply, so always check the current consolidated text.

section: Section 22-A Powers of Justice of the Peace
text: If the police refuse to register your complaint, one commonly used remedy is to apply to the Justice of the Peace (usually a Sessions Judge acting in that role), who can examine the matter and issue directions. Read the current text and case law with a lawyer.

section: Section 61 Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours
text: A police officer cannot keep an arrested person in custody for more than 24 hours (excluding travel time to court) without a magistrate's order. It works together with Article 10 of the Constitution.

This is the section on the First Information Report (FIR). When someone gives information to the police about a cognizable offence (a serious offence where police can act without a warrant), the police must record it and the informant should be given a copy. The FIR starts the investigation.

section: Section 167 Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours
text: If the investigation cannot be finished within 24 hours, the police present the accused before a magistrate, who may allow physical remand (police custody) for a limited period or send the accused to judicial custody.

section: Section 173 Report of police officer on completion of investigation
text: When the investigation ends, the police submit a report (commonly called the challan) to the court stating whether they found enough evidence to send the accused for trial.

section: Section 496 In what cases bail to be taken
text: When a person is accused of a bailable offence, they can get bail as a matter of right. The police or the court must release them if they are ready to give bail.

section: Section 497 When bail may be taken in case of non-bailable offence
text: For serious (non-bailable) offences, bail is not a right: the court decides on the facts, looking at whether there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused committed the offence and other factors. Courts treat cases involving women, minors and the sick or infirm with special consideration.

section: Section 498 Power to direct admission to bail or reduction of bail
text: Gives the High Court and the Court of Session power to grant bail, including the commonly used “pre-arrest bail” (protective bail before arrest) where the court is satisfied that the case calls for it, and to reduce bail amounts. Read the current text and case law with a lawyer.
The law of evidence: what a court accepts as proof, who must prove what, how witnesses are examined and how documents (including electronic records) are treated.

Sets out the structure, duties and accountability of the police and includes provisions for complaints against police misconduct. Different provinces have since adopted their own police laws, so check which law applies where you live.
The main law on driving licences, vehicle registration, road rules and traffic offences. Provinces issue their own rules, fines and e-challan systems under it, so penalties differ by location.

The procedural law for civil cases (disputes about money, property, contracts and rights): how to file a suit, serve notice, get temporary orders such as injunctions, and enforce a decree. Provinces have made some local amendments.

section: Section 9 Courts to try all civil suits unless barred
text: Civil courts can hear every civil dispute unless the law expressly or by clear implication takes it away from them. If you have a civil right and nobody else has been given the power to decide, the civil court is usually the place to go.

section: Section 80 Notice before suing the Government or a public officer
text: Before suing the Government or a public officer for something done in an official capacity, a written notice generally has to be given and a waiting period must pass, with limited exceptions. Check the current text for the waiting period and exceptions.

section: Order XXXVII Summary procedure on negotiable instruments
text: A faster “summary suit” route for recovering money based on certain documents such as cheques, bills of exchange and promissory notes. The defendant needs the court's permission to defend. Check the current text and your province's amendments.

section: Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 Temporary injunctions
text: Lets a court order someone to stop (or sometimes do) something while the main case is pending — for example, to stop a person from selling or building on disputed property. The applicant usually has to show a prima facie case, that harm would be hard to undo, and that the balance of convenience favours them.
Explains when a promise or agreement becomes a legally enforceable contract, what makes it valid or void, and what remedies (such as compensation) are available for breach.

Agreements are contracts when the parties are competent to contract, freely consent, have a lawful object and lawful consideration (something of value exchanged), and are not expressly declared void. Some contracts must also be in writing or registered.

section: Section 73 Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract
text: If one party breaks a contract, the other can claim compensation for the loss that naturally arose from the breach (or that both sides knew was likely). It does not cover remote or indirect losses.
Allows courts to declare rights and to order a person to do (specific performance) or stop doing (injunction) something, instead of only awarding money. Used in many property and contract disputes.

section: Section 42 Discretion of court as to declaration of status or right
text: A person with a legal right or character who is denied it can ask the court for a declaration (a formal statement) of that right — for example, a declaration of ownership. The court has discretion and will not grant it if a further relief could have been asked but wasn't.

After a full hearing, a court can permanently forbid someone from violating your legal right (for example from interfering with your possession of property). It differs from a temporary injunction, which lasts only while the case is pending.
Sets the time limits within which a suit, appeal or application must be filed. Missing a deadline can end a claim, so check the limit that applies to your type of case as early as possible.
Governs how immovable property (land, houses) is transferred: sale, mortgage, lease, gift and exchange. It defines these transactions and says when documents must be written and registered.

A sale transfers ownership of property for a price. For property of higher value, the transfer is made only by a registered instrument; for very low-value property, delivery of possession may be enough. Check the current monetary limits and your province's registration rules.

A lease transfers the right to enjoy property for a time in return for rent or another price. The giver is the lessor (landlord) and the taker is the lessee (tenant). Rented-premises laws of each province add specific tenant and landlord rules.

A lease of immovable property for more than one year must be made by a registered instrument; shorter leases can be made by a registered instrument or by delivery of possession. A written, registered tenancy agreement is safer for both sides.
Explains which documents must be registered (such as many sale deeds and long leases), where and when to register them, and why registration protects your title.

section: Section 17 Documents of which registration is compulsory
text: Lists documents that must be registered to be effective — for example, instruments that create or transfer rights in immovable property above a stated value, and leases for more than one year. An unregistered document of this kind may not be accepted as proof of the transaction.
The main tenancy law in Sindh: fair rent, tenant and landlord duties, the grounds on which a landlord can seek eviction, and the Rent Controller who decides such disputes.
The tenancy law in Punjab. It covers tenancy agreements, rent, eviction and the Rent Tribunal. Check the current text for registration of tenancy agreements and eviction procedure.
The tenancy law for Islamabad Capital Territory covering rent, eviction and the Rent Controller.

Regulates several matters for Muslims: registration of marriage, notice and procedure for talaq, restrictions on a second marriage, maintenance, and the share of grandchildren whose parent died before the grandparent. It applies to Muslim citizens; other communities have their own personal laws.

If a son or daughter dies before their parent, that person's children (the grandchildren) are treated as inheriting the share their parent would have received from the grandparent. Read the full section for the conditions.

A Muslim marriage should be registered with the Union Council (or the relevant local authority). The Nikah Registrar who solemnises the marriage must record it in the prescribed form and give a copy to the parties. A registered nikahnama is key proof of marriage, dower and conditions.

A man who already has a wife must not contract another marriage without first applying for written permission from the Arbitration Council and the application must state whether the existing wife's consent has been obtained. Marrying without permission has legal consequences. Check the current text.

A man who pronounces talaq must give written notice to the Chairman of the Union Council and supply a copy to his wife. The Council then tries reconciliation, and under this section the talaq generally takes effect after a waiting period (ninety days from the notice, unless the wife is pregnant, in which case the rules differ). Read the exact text.

If a husband fails to maintain his wife (or fails to treat co-wives equitably), the wife can apply to the Chairman of the Union Council, which can decide on maintenance. Many maintenance claims are also brought in the Family Court. Read the current text.

Lists the grounds on which a Muslim woman can ask a court to dissolve her marriage (for example, if the husband's whereabouts are unknown, he fails to maintain her, or treats her with cruelty). It works alongside the right to khula and the Family Courts Act, 1964.

section: Section 2 Grounds for decree for dissolution of marriage
text: A woman married under Muslim law can seek a decree dissolving her marriage on specific grounds, such as the husband being missing for a period, failing to provide maintenance, imprisonment for a long term, failing to perform marital obligations, cruelty, and certain other grounds listed in the section. Read the exact list and time periods in the official text.

Creates Family Courts that hear marriage, dissolution (including khula), dower, maintenance, custody of children and related disputes. It requires the court to attempt reconciliation and aims at quicker, simpler procedure than ordinary civil courts.

Family Courts have exclusive jurisdiction over the matters listed in the Schedule to the Act, such as dissolution of marriage (including khula), dower, maintenance, restitution of conjugal rights, custody and guardianship of children, and the return of dowry or bridal gifts. Check the current Schedule.

Before and during a family case the court is required to try to bring the parties to a compromise. In suits for dissolution of marriage the court has particular duties to attempt reconciliation, and in a khula case the court's powers and the effect on dower are set out in this section. Read the exact text.
Governs the appointment of guardians for minors and decisions about their custody. Courts treat the welfare of the child as the leading consideration.

section: Section 17 Matters to be considered by the court in appointing guardian
text: In appointing a guardian the court considers what is for the welfare of the minor, taking into account the minor's age, sex and religion, the character and capacity of the proposed guardian, existing relationships, and the minor's own preference if old enough to form one.

section: Section 25 Title of guardian to custody of ward
text: If a ward leaves or is removed from the custody of the guardian, the court can order the ward to be returned if it is for the ward's welfare. Welfare of the child, not the parents' preference, is the central test.
Limits dowry and bridal gifts and requires that gifts given to the bride be treated as her property. Disputes about return of dowry and gifts commonly go to the Family Court.

Provides rules on inheritance by will and on intestate succession for people to whom it applies, primarily non-Muslims. Muslim inheritance follows Islamic personal law as applied in Pakistan (see MFLO 1961, Section 4).

Provincial law in Sindh that restrains child marriage and sets the minimum marriage age at 18 for both boys and girls, with penalties. Rules differ in other provinces, so check the law for your own province.

Requires employers to pay wages on time and limits deductions from wages. A worker whose wages are delayed or wrongly deducted can claim before the authority appointed under the Act. Provinces have their own versions or amendments.

Covers trade unions, collective bargaining, industrial disputes and unfair labour practices in establishments to which it applies (mainly in Islamabad and inter-provincial establishments). Provinces have their own industrial relations laws for provincial matters.

law: Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015
text: Sets basic terms of employment in covered Sindh establishments: appointment letters, working conditions, leave, misconduct procedures and termination. Check the current text for who is covered.

Protects consumers in Sindh against defective goods, deficient services and unfair practices, and provides for Consumer Courts where a consumer can file a complaint. Check the current text for the procedure and time limits.
Protects consumers in Punjab and provides for Consumer Courts. It covers defective products, misleading advertisements and poor service. Check the current text for time limits.

law: Islamabad Capital Territory Consumer Protection Act, 1995
text: Consumer protection law for Islamabad Capital Territory, covering defective goods and unfair practices and providing a complaint process.

law: Establishment of the Office of Wafaqi Mohtasib (Ombudsman) Order, 1983
text: Creates the Federal Ombudsman (Wafaqi Mohtasib), an office where anyone can complain free of charge about maladministration by federal government agencies — for example delay, neglect, or unfair treatment. Provinces have their own Ombudsman offices for provincial departments.

Defines cyber offences such as unauthorised access to systems and data, identity misuse, offences against the dignity and modesty of a person, and cyber stalking, and sets out investigation powers and procedure. It was amended in 2025; always check the current consolidated text.

section: Section 16 Unauthorised use of identity information
text: Using, obtaining or selling another person's identity information (for example, a CNIC number or photographs) without authority and for gain or harm can be an offence. Section numbering should be confirmed in the current text.

section: Section 20 Offences against dignity of a natural person
text: Intentionally publishing or displaying false or intimidating information about a person that harms their reputation or privacy can be an offence. Check the current text and amendments.

section: Section 21 Offences against modesty of a natural person and minor
text: Covers sharing or threatening to share sexually explicit or manipulated images of a person, including for blackmail. Victims can complain to the FIA's cybercrime wing. Check the current text.
Repeatedly following, contacting, monitoring or harassing a person through the internet or other electronic means, causing fear or distress, can be cyber stalking. Check the current text.

law: Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010
text: Requires organisations to adopt a code of conduct and set up an Inquiry Committee for harassment complaints, and allows complaints to the Ombudsman (federal or provincial). It protects the person complaining from retaliation. Check the current text and any later amendments on the official portal.

law: Sindh Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act, 2013
text: Provides protection against domestic violence in Sindh, including protection orders, residence and monetary relief, and a complaint mechanism. Check the current text and how it is implemented in your district.

law: Punjab Protection of Women against Violence Act, 2016
text: Provides protection for women against violence in Punjab, including protection orders and a complaint process and shelters. Check the current text.

law: Legal Aid and Justice Authority Act, 2020
text: Establishes a federal authority to provide legal aid to people who cannot afford a lawyer, particularly vulnerable groups. Check the current text and the authority's website for how to apply and which cases are covered.

law: Right of Access to Information Act, 2017
text: Lets citizens request records held by federal public bodies. A public body must respond within a set time, and a refusal can be taken to the Information Commission. It does not cover provincial departments, which have their own right-to-information laws.

law: Sindh Transparency and Right to Information Act, 2016
text: The right-to-information law for Sindh public bodies: how to request records and how to complain to the Sindh Information Commission if refused.

law: Punjab Transparency and Right to Information Act, 2013
text: The right-to-information law for Punjab public bodies, including how to request records and appeal to the Punjab Information Commission.

law: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Right to Information Act, 2013
text: The right-to-information law for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa public bodies, including how to request records and complain to the Information Commission.
Bail / ضمانت / ضمانت: Temporary release of an accused person from custody on a promise to attend court, usually with a bond or sureties.

FIR (First Information Report) / ایف آئی آر (ابتدائی اطلاعی رپورٹ) / ايف آءِ آر (پهرين اطلاعي رپورٽ): The first written police record of information about a cognizable offence, which starts an investigation.
Surety / ضامن / ضامن: A person who promises the court that an accused person will attend hearings and who may forfeit money if they do not.
Warrant / وارنٹ / وارنٽ: A written order from a court authorising the police to arrest a person or search a place.
Summons / سمن / سمن: A court notice requiring a person to appear in court or produce a document on a stated date.
Evidence / شہادت / ثبوت / شاهدي / ثبوت: Statements, documents and objects a court accepts to decide whether a fact is proved.
Witness / گواہ / شاهد: A person who tells the court what they saw, heard or know about the case.
Appeal / اپیل / اپيل: A request to a higher court to review and change a decision of a lower court.
Injunction / حکمِ امتناعی / حڪمِ امتناعي: A court order requiring a person to do, or stop doing, a specific act.
Contract / معاہدہ / معاهدو: A legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties.
Inheritance / وراثت / وراثت: Property that passes to the legal heirs of a person after death.
Maintenance / نان نفقہ / نان نفقو: Financial support a person is legally required to provide to a spouse or child, such as food, clothing and housing.
Custody / تحویل / حضانت / سنڀال / حضانت: The legal right and responsibility to care for and have the day-to-day charge of a child.
Dower (Mehr) / حق مہر / حق مهر: The sum or property a husband agrees or is bound to give his wife under the marriage contract.
Divorce / طلاق / طلاق: The legal ending of a marriage, by talaq, court decree or khula.
Khula / خلع / خلع: Dissolution of marriage sought by the wife, decided by the Family Court.
Nikah / نکاح / نڪاح: The Muslim marriage contract.
Jurisdiction / دائرۂ اختیار / دائرو اختيار: The authority of a court or law to decide a matter — based on the subject, the value, the place or the people involved.
Arrest / گرفتاری / گرفتاري: Taking a person into custody by lawful authority, usually on suspicion of an offence.
Remand / ریمانڈ / ريمانڊ: An order of a magistrate sending an accused person to police or judicial custody for a limited period during investigation.
Cognizable offence / قابلِ دست اندازیٔ پولیس جرم / قابلِ دست اندازيءَ پوليس ڏوهه: A serious offence for which police may arrest and investigate without a court's prior permission.
Tenant / کرایہ دار / ڪرائيدار: A person who rents property from its owner (the landlord) in return for rent.
Plaintiff / مدعی / مدعي: The person who files a civil suit.
Defendant / مدعا علیہ / مدعا عليه: The person against whom a civil suit is filed.
Writ / رٹ / رٽ: A written court order directing a person or authority to act or stop acting, issued by the High Court under Article 199.
Habeas corpus / حبسِ بے جا (ہیبیس کارپس) / هيبيس ڪارپس: A writ requiring a person who is detained to be brought before the court so that the lawfulness of the detention can be checked.
Right to information / حقِ معلومات / ڄاڻ جو حق: The right of citizens to request records held by public bodies, subject to limited exceptions.
Harassment / ہراسانی / تنگ ڪرڻ (هراسانگي): Unwelcome conduct, words or messages that cause fear, humiliation or distress, including in the workplace or online.
Cheating / دھوکا دہی / ٺڳي: Deceiving a person so that they dishonestly hand over property or sign a valuable document.
Equality before law / قانون کے سامنے برابری / قانون آڏو برابري: The principle that all citizens are subject to the same law and entitled to equal protection of the law (Article 25).

section: What can I do if a government authority violates my fundamental rights?
text: What can I do if a government authority violates my fundamental rights? First raise the issue with the authority in writing and, where available, with an ombudsman or appeal authority. If there is no other adequate remedy, a constitutional petition can be filed in the High Court under Article 199. A lawyer or a legal-aid office can help you prepare it.

section: Does equality before the law mean women and men are treated identically?
text: Does equality before the law mean women and men are treated identically? Article 25 says all citizens are equal before the law and there is no discrimination on the basis of sex alone. It also allows the State to make special provisions to protect women and children, which are not treated as prohibited discrimination.

section: Why does the law differ between provinces?
text: Why does the law differ between provinces? Pakistan has federal laws and provincial laws. Many everyday subjects — such as tenancy, consumer protection and local services — are mainly dealt with by provincial legislation, so the rules in Sindh can differ from those in Punjab or Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Select your province on this site to see the most relevant laws first.

section: Which court should I go to?
text: Which court should I go to? It depends on the type of case and its value or seriousness. Criminal cases start before a magistrate or sessions court; civil money and property suits go to civil courts; family matters go to the Family Court; rent, consumer and labour disputes often have their own tribunals or courts. A lawyer or the court's office can confirm the correct forum.

section: How do I register an FIR?
text: How do I register an FIR? Go to the police station and give the police the information about the offence — what happened, when, where and who was involved. For a cognizable offence the police must record it under Section 154 of the CrPC. Ask for a copy of the FIR; the informant is entitled to one. Avoid exaggeration: a knowingly false report can itself be an offence.

section: What if the police refuse to register my FIR?
text: What if the police refuse to register my FIR? Put your complaint in writing, send it to the senior police officer of the district, and keep proof. You can also approach the Justice of the Peace (Section 22-A CrPC) to seek directions. A lawyer or legal-aid office can help prepare the application.

section: What are my rights if I am arrested?
text: What are my rights if I am arrested? Under Article 10 of the Constitution you must be told the grounds of arrest as soon as possible, you may consult and be defended by a lawyer of your choice, and you must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time). Article 14 prohibits torture to extract evidence. Special rules apply to preventive detention.

What is remand? If an investigation cannot be completed within 24 hours, the police present the accused before a magistrate (Section 167 CrPC). The magistrate may allow a limited period of physical remand to the police or send the accused to judicial custody. The accused can ask to be examined by a doctor and should tell the magistrate about any ill-treatment.

section: What is bail and how do I apply for it?
text: What is bail and how do I apply for it? Bail is the temporary release of an accused person from custody on a promise (usually with sureties or a bond) to attend court. A lawyer files a bail application before the court that has jurisdiction — the magistrate, the Sessions Court or the High Court, depending on the offence and stage. For bailable offences bail is a matter of right (Section 496 CrPC); for non-bailable offences the court decides on the facts (Section 497).

What is pre-arrest bail? Pre-arrest (anticipatory) bail is protection granted by a court before arrest, usually under Section 498 CrPC, where a person fears arrest on a false or malicious accusation. It is not automatic: the court looks closely at the facts. Seek a lawyer's advice quickly because the person must usually appear before the court.

section: How do I register a nikah?
text: How do I register a nikah? A Muslim marriage should be registered under Section 5 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961. The Nikah Registrar who solemnises the nikah records it in the nikahnama and sends the record to the Union Council. Make sure every column — including dower and any conditions — is filled in before signing, and keep your copy safe.

section: What is the legal minimum age for marriage?
text: What is the legal minimum age for marriage? It depends on the province or territory. For example, Sindh's Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2013 sets the minimum age at 18 for both boys and girls. Other jurisdictions have different laws, so check the law for where you live before relying on any age.

section: How can a woman seek khula or divorce?
text: How can a woman seek khula or divorce? A wife can file a suit for dissolution of marriage in the Family Court of the area where she lives. She may seek khula (dissolution on the basis that she no longer wishes to continue the marriage) or dissolution on one of the grounds listed in the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 (for example cruelty or failure to maintain). The court first tries reconciliation; the effect of khula on dower is addressed by law and case law, so get legal advice.

How does talaq work legally? Under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, a man who pronounces talaq must give written notice to the Chairman of the Union Council and supply a copy to the wife. The Council attempts reconciliation, and generally the talaq takes effect after the waiting period set by the law. Failure to give notice can be an offence. Ask the Union Council for a certificate recording the outcome.

section: How can a wife or child claim maintenance?
text: How can a wife or child claim maintenance? Maintenance claims are commonly filed in the Family Court. A wife can also apply to the Union Council Chairman under Section 9 of the MFLO if her husband fails to maintain her. Keep proof of the relationship, the husband's income and your own expenses; courts can order interim maintenance while the case is pending.

section: What if my dower has not been paid?
text: What if my dower has not been paid? Dower (mehr) belongs to the wife and is a debt owed by the husband. It may be “prompt” (payable on demand) or “deferred” (payable later, often on divorce or death), as recorded in the nikahnama. A claim for unpaid dower can be filed in the Family Court. Keep the nikahnama safe — it is the key evidence.

section: Who gets custody of the children after separation?
text: Who gets custody of the children after separation? The court decides on the welfare of the child, considering age, needs, upbringing, the capacity of each parent and the child's wishes if old enough. Personal-law principles on custody are considered, especially for young children, but welfare is the governing test (Guardians and Wards Act, 1890). A custody order can be revisited if circumstances change.

section: What do I need to claim my share of inheritance?
text: What do I need to claim my share of inheritance? Typically a death certificate, proof of the relationship of all legal heirs (for example a family registration certificate or legal-heirs certificate), and documents of the property (title, registry, revenue record). Property in revenue records is normally updated through an inheritance mutation. If heirs disagree, a civil suit for declaration and partition may be needed. Requirements vary by province.

section: Do grandchildren inherit if their parent died before the grandparent?
text: Do grandchildren inherit if their parent died before the grandparent? Section 4 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 provides that the children of a son or daughter who died before the grandparent take the share their parent would have received. Read the full section for conditions; for non-Muslims the Succession Act, 1925 and their personal law apply.

section: What is a legal notice for money recovery?
text: What is a legal notice for money recovery? A legal notice is a written demand, usually sent through a lawyer, telling the other person what you claim and giving a reasonable time to pay or respond. It is often not legally required before a suit (notice to the Government under CPC Section 80 is a specific exception), but it can help settlement and shows the court you gave a chance to resolve the matter.

section: What can I do if a cheque given to me bounces?
text: What can I do if a cheque given to me bounces? Keep the original cheque and the bank's return memo. Possible routes include a civil summary suit for recovery (CPC Order XXXVII) and, where the facts fit, a criminal complaint for dishonestly issuing a cheque under the Pakistan Penal Code. Time limits apply, so speak to a lawyer promptly.

section: Can a landlord throw out a tenant without a court order?
text: Can a landlord throw out a tenant without a court order? In general, no. Provincial rented-premises laws provide a legal process: the landlord applies to the Rent Controller or Rent Tribunal on one of the grounds allowed by law (for example non-payment of rent, subletting or genuine personal need), and the tenant is heard. Forcibly removing a tenant or cutting off essential services can itself create legal problems for the landlord. The exact grounds differ between Sindh, Punjab and Islamabad.

section: Do I need a written tenancy agreement?
text: Do I need a written tenancy agreement? A written agreement is strongly advisable. A lease of immovable property for more than one year must be by registered instrument (Transfer of Property Act, Section 107), and some provinces have specific tenancy-agreement or registration rules. A clear agreement stating rent, advance, duration, repairs and notice makes disputes much easier to resolve.

section: What should I check before buying property?
text: What should I check before buying property? Verify that the seller is the true owner (title documents and the official revenue or registry record), check for existing mortgages, disputes or court cases, confirm the property's description and boundaries, and make sure the sale is completed by a registered sale deed followed by mutation in the record. Pay by traceable bank instruments and keep every receipt. Use a lawyer for due diligence.

section: What can I do if my employer does not pay my wages?
text: What can I do if my employer does not pay my wages? Ask for payment in writing and keep proof of your work and agreed pay (appointment letter, messages, attendance, payslips). If unpaid, complain to the labour department or the authority under the wages law that applies to your workplace — for example the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 as applied in your province — or a labour court. Time limits apply, so act soon.

section: Can my employer terminate me without notice?
text: Can my employer terminate me without notice? It depends on your contract and the labour law that applies (for example the Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 for covered Sindh establishments). Covered workers are usually entitled to notice or pay in lieu and, for misconduct, to a fair procedure. Keep your appointment letter and speak to the labour department or a lawyer quickly.

section: How do I complain about a defective product or poor service?
text: How do I complain about a defective product or poor service? Keep the receipt, warranty and any advertisement. Complain to the seller or provider in writing and give them a reasonable time to fix, replace or refund. If unresolved, you can approach the Consumer Court under your province's consumer protection law (for example the Sindh Consumer Protection Act, 2014 or the Punjab Consumer Protection Act, 2005). Check the time limit and the required notice.

section: What should I do if I am being harassed or blackmailed online?
text: What should I do if I am being harassed or blackmailed online? Do not delete anything. Take screenshots showing the account, messages, dates and URLs, and save them in more than one place. Do not pay or comply with threats. Report the content to the platform and complain to the FIA's cybercrime wing (NR3C) or your nearest police station; the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 covers offences such as cyber stalking and offences against modesty and dignity. Reach out to a trusted person or a legal-aid or support organisation.

section: What should I do if I receive a traffic challan I disagree with?
text: What should I do if I receive a traffic challan I disagree with? Read the challan carefully: the offence, date, location and amount. Most provinces let you pay at designated banks or online, and also let you contest it before the traffic court or magistrate within a stated time. Keep your licence, registration and the challan copy, and check the process with your provincial traffic police or authority because fines and procedures differ.

section: How do I request information from a government office?
text: How do I request information from a government office? Send a written request to the public body's designated information officer, describing the record you want as precisely as you can and giving your contact details. The law sets a deadline for a reply and allows fees only for copying. If your request is refused or ignored, you can complain to the relevant Information Commission. Use the right law: the federal Right of Access to Information Act, 2017 covers federal bodies; provinces have their own laws.

section: What if I cannot afford a lawyer?
text: What if I cannot afford a lawyer? Legal aid exists for people who cannot afford a lawyer. The Legal Aid and Justice Authority Act, 2020 created a federal authority for this, and many district bar associations and courts run legal-aid committees or panels of lawyers. In criminal cases, ask the court whether a lawyer can be provided. Bring your CNIC and case papers, and verify the current procedure at the authority's office or website.
